feed.title: Debezium
feed.subtitle: Debezium is an open source distributed platform for change data capture. Start it up, point it at your databases, and your apps can start responding to all of the inserts, updates, and deletes that other apps commit to your databases. Debezium is durable and fast, so your apps can respond quickly and never miss an event, even when things go wrong.

entry.title: Debezium 3.3.2.Final Released
entry.content:
Debezium 3.3.2.Final is now available with important fixes and stability improvements across multiple database connectors.

In this post, we’re going to take a deep dive into the improvements made across several key modules of Debezium, discussing any new features, and explaining any changes that could impact your upgrade process. As always, we recommend you read the release notes to learn about all the bugs that were fixed, update procedures, and more.

New features and improvements

Let’s cover some noteworthy improvements and changes in 3.3.2.Final.

PostgreSQL connector compatibility fixed for Java 23+

When running Debezium using JDK23+, sometimes when parsing timestamp values from PostgreSQL they could lead to NullPointerException errors. To address this compatibility issue, we have made some adjustments so that later JDK builds do now lead to these obscure failures (DBZ-9558).

Oracle low watermark calculation no longer causes performance loss

When an Oracle LogMiner mining step completes, the Debezium Oracle connector needs to calculate the next starting position for mining. When lob.enabled is set to false (the default), it was observed that this calculation was too conservative, and could lead to a regression in performance.

This regression has been fixed, and the connector should once again resume reading changes without the low watermark calculation causing performance loss (DBZ-9664).

Oracle heartbeats no longer stop when mining returns no data

The Debezium Oracle connector recently introduced an experimental feature using Common Table Expression (CTE) queries to allow another way to optimize the data fetch from Oracle LogMiner. However, the community reported that when using this feature, if the query returned no events, Debezium stopped emitting heartbeat events.

This has been fixed, and users should observe that heartbeat events should always be emitted by the Oracle connector, even if the mining pass fetched no data (DBZ-9443).

SQL Server incremental snapshots now resume after restart

When an incremental snapshot was in progress for a SQL Server connector, if a rebalance or connector restart was triggered for any reason, any in-progress incremental snapshot would fail to resume upon restart. This is unintended and was due to regression in the handling of the connector’s offsets during incremental snapshots.

This issue is fixed for SQL Sever, and we identified that no other connector was impacted by this regression. SQL Server users should now observe that if the connector is restarted during an incremental snapshot, the snapshot resumes upon restart as intended (DBZ-9533).

OpenLineage can now be fully disabled

Several users reported issues when openlineage.integration.enabled was set to false, Debezium was still trying to resolve OpenLineage features in some parts of the code, which could lead to undesirable IllegalStateException errors while trying to initialize OpenLineage.

This issue is resolved and Debezium fully respects the openlineage.integration.enabled property and will not attempt to perform any OpenLineage setup or initialization when set to false (DBZ-9504).

Other fixes

  • Can bind a LONG value only for insert into a LONG column DBZ-8276

  • DdlChanges not reset in schema history recovery DBZ-9549

  • Skipped events counter not handled correctly for compressed transactions DBZ-9564

  • Handle exceptions thrown from perfromCommit method to gracefully cleanup the coordinator during the stop call DBZ-9617

  • Table column metadata is not fetched when table name has a '/' character DBZ-9620

  • MySQL connector does not parse CREATE TABLE DBZ-9623

  • Debezium Server run.bat fails to execute on Windows DBZ-9625

  • Begin marker but no end marker for rollbacked transactions DBZ-9628

  • MariaDB fails to parse "CONVERT TO CHARSET <character-set>" DBZ-9634

  • Oracle does not support renaming partitions using alter table DBZ-9651

  • MongoDB connector: Whitespace in collection.include.list causes incorrect regex pattern in change streams DBZ-9657

  • Debezium Oracle restarting mining session too frequently DBZ-9680

  • Debezium Oracle connector fails to parse Oracle database version DBZ-9681

  • MySQLGTIDSet Subtractions Fail on UUIDSet that exist only in the Left Operand DBZ-9682

  • NPE during sending to HTTP sink DBZ-9698

In total, 21 issues were resolved in Debezium 3.3.2.Final. The list of changes can also be found in our release notes.

A big thank you to all the contributors from the community who worked diligently on this release:
Animesh Kumar, Artem Shubovych, Auke van Leeuwen, Chris Cranford, Daniel Eriksson, Guangnan Shi, Hagar Yasser, Hong Xia, Jiri Pechanec, Kaustuv Chakrabarti, Lars M. Johansson, Olivier Chédru, Poonam Meghnani, Rajendra Dangwal, Robert Roldan, rptroberts, and Sumit Jha!

entry.title: Debezium 3.4.0.Beta1 Released
entry.content:
We are nearing the end of the quarter, and we’re excited to announce that the next preview build of Debezium is available, 3.4.0.Beta1. This release introduces support for extended authentication modes, timezone conversion support for source info block fields, and numerous improvements and enhancements to the Debezium connector portfolio. Let’s take a few moments and look at what are some of the highlights.

Breaking changes

With any new major release of software, there is often several breaking changes. The Debezium 3.4.0.Beta1 release is no exception, so let’s discuss the major changes you should be aware of.

Configurable PostgreSQL flush strategy changes

A new configuration option was added for PostgreSQL users called lsn.flush.mode. This option provides more control over the replication slot flush strategy (DBZ-9641). This configuration option replaces flush.lsn.source, which is now deprecated and will be removed in a future update.

New features and improvements

The following describes all noteworthy new features and improvements in Debezium 3.4.0.Beta1. For a complete list, be sure to read the release notes for more details.

AWS IAM authentication support for PostgreSQL

Debezium 3.4 introduces the ability to specify user credentials that must be validated using AWS IAM authentication. This feature, while present for MySQL, is now available for PostgreSQL connector users.

Prerequisites

  • Add the AWS Advanced JDBC Wrapper to your connector’s plugin directory or class path.
    You can find more information about this process here.

  • Add the connector configuration property database.connection.factory.class in the connector configuration.
    Set the value to io.debezium.connector.postgresql.connection.PostgresAwsIamConnectionFactory.

With this configuration, the connector credentials will be validated against AWS IAM rather than the database (DBZ-7297).

Timezone conversion support for source info block fields

The ConvertTimezone SMT has been a great addition for specific use cases where the community has wanted to shift the values of timestamps by timezone offsets. However, this transformation’s capabilities were limited to very specific Debezium logical field types.

One request from the community was to extend this transformation to support for additional fields in the Debezium event’s source information block. Debezium 3.4 adds the ts_ms, ts_us, and ts_ns fields from the source information block as eligible fields that can be converted (DBZ-9372).

Please see the ConvertTimezone documentation for more details.

Support MongoDB wall clock time

In MongoDB 6+, wallTime was added to MongoDB change stream events to represent the server’s date and time when a database operation occurred, specifically when the transaction was committed or the operation completed. This is slightly different from clusterTime, which is when the entry was added to the database’s oplog.

With Debezium 3.4, the ts_ms, ts_us, and ts_ns source information block fields will be based on the wallTime if it’s available in the change event, falling back to clusterTime when it’s unavailable (DBZ-9683).

Improved PostgreSQL LSN flushing strategy

In previous versions of Debezium for PostgreSQL, typically users would allow Debezium to control when the LSN was flushed to the replication slot using flush.lsn.source; however, users could set this false and control the flush manually outside of Debezium.

Starting with Debezium 3.4, a new connector configuration lsn.flush.mode was added to provide an extended way to control how the LSN is flushed to PostgreSQL during the connector’s lifecycle (DBZ-9641). This new property can be set to one of the following options:

connector

Specifies that the Debezium PostgreSQL connector controls when the LSN is flushed to the replication slot. This is the same behavior as the deprecated flush.lsn.source option when set to true.

manual

Specifies that the Debezium PostgreSQL connector no longer controls when the LSN is flushed to the replication slot and that it must be performed manually or externally to the connector. This is the same behavior as the deprecated flush.lsn.source option when set to false.

connector_and_driver

Specifies a new mode where both the Debezium PostgreSQL connector and the PostgreSQL JDBC driver manage when the LSN is flushed to the replication slot. Debezium will flush as it processes events while the driver will flush during idle periods based on the server keepalive messages.

Support Oracle’s subset database replication logging mode

Debezium has long recommended that the best supplemental logging mode is to enable minimum supplemental logging mode at the database level and then specify all column logging on a per-table basis. This minimizes the volume of data recorded in your database transaction logs and improves the overall performance of Debezium.

In Oracle 21, a new supplemental logging mode was introduced called SUBSET DATABASE REPLICATION, which replaces the the previously used Minimum Supplemental Logging Mode.

In Debezium 3.4, the Debezium Oracle connector recognizes this new logging mode as an equivalent to the minimum supplemental logging mode, allowing users to set one or the other rather than both (DBZ-7341), simplifying the setup required for capturing changes using LogMiner.

Discard Oracle in-progress transactions manually

Debezium’s Oracle connector is a bit unique in that it must buffer all events for a transaction before the transaction can be emitted as change events when using LogMiner. In some situations, users have found themselves in a situation where a transaction is being buffered, but it’s not something they care about. Currently, you need to wait for the transaction commit or rollback to be observed or the transaction buffer retention to be met. In some environments, this is less than ideal.

Debezium 3.4 introduces a new special Oracle signal called drop-transaction, that allows you to specifically discard an in-progress transaction that is currently being buffered (DBZ-9552).

Example discard transaction signal
INSERT INTO the_signal_table
VALUES ('my-signal-id', 'drop-transaction', '{"transaction-id": "<the-database-trx-id>"}');

When this signal is processed, Debezium will locate the transaction in the buffer, and if it exists, the transaction will be abandoned immediately rather than waiting for the transaction buffer retention if configured.

Configurable Oracle session hash/sort area values

An Oracle database is configured by database administrators with a variety of session default values, many of which control the amount of resources the connection can consume when executing queries or running PL/SQL programs. Two very specific database parameters are:

hash_area_size

This specifies the maximum amount of memory, in bytes, to be used when performing hash joins.

sort_area_size

This specifies the maximum amount of memory, in bytes, to be used when performing query sorts.

Normally these values are set automatically by the database sizing configuration and should not be altered; however, there are some corner cases where adjusting these values larger can help improve specific queries and performance, including the log mining pass used by Debezium.

To adjust these two options, the Debezium Oracle connector provides two internal, experimental properties:

internal.log.mining.hash.area.size

Specifies the maximum amount of memory, in bytes, to be used for hash joins.

internal.log.mining.sort.area.size

Specifies the maximum amount of memory, in bytes, to be used for query sorts.

Careful consideration should be taken before explicitly setting these configuration options. In situations where these values are set too large, they can create stability issues in the database.

You should consult your database administrator before setting either of these.

Oracle low watermark calculation no longer causes performance loss

When an Oracle LogMiner mining step completes, the Debezium Oracle connector needs to calculate the next starting position for mining. When lob.enabled is set to false (the default), it was observed that this calculation was too conservative, and could lead to a regression in performance.

This regression has been fixed, and the connector should once again resume reading changes without the low watermark calculation causing performance loss (DBZ-9664).

Oracle heartbeats no longer stop when mining returns no data

The Debezium Oracle connector recently introduced an experimental feature using Common Table Expression (CTE) queries to allow another way to optimize the data fetch from Oracle LogMiner. However, the community reported that when using this feature, if the query returned no events, Debezium stopped emitting heartbeat events.

This has been fixed, and users should observe that heartbeat events should always be emitted by the Oracle connector, even if the mining pass fetched no data (DBZ-9443).

SQL Server incremental snapshots now resume after restart

When an incremental snapshot was in progress for a SQL Server connector, if a rebalance or connector restart was triggered for any reason, any in-progress incremental snapshot would fail to resume upon restart. This is unintended and was due to regression in the handling of the connector’s offsets during incremental snapshots.

This issue is fixed for SQL Sever, and we identified that no other connector was impacted by this regression. SQL Server users should now observe that if the connector is restarted during an incremental snapshot, the snapshot resumes upon restart as intended (DBZ-9533).

Selectively target tables during Vitess copy phase

New JDBC connector passthrough collection naming strategy

While the Debezium JDBC connector is purpose-built to consume Debezium change events without the ExtractNewRecordState transformation, some use cases require it anyway. This creates a challenge: you may want to use the ${source.*} pattern with collection.naming.format to map events to your target tables. But with the source information block stripped away, this approach no longer works.

To solve this problem and streamline deployments that need this capability, the JDBC sink connector now includes a passthrough collection naming strategy. This strategy uses the event’s topic name directly, without any sanitization, as the target table name (DBZ-9679). It enables you to pair other transformations that modify the topic name with precise control over how events map to tables.

To enable the passthrough collection naming strategy, add this to your connector configuration:

{
  "collection.naming.strategy": "io.debezium.sink.naming.PassthroughCollectionNamingStrategy"
}

With this strategy, events from topic public.orders will be written directly to a table named public.orders.

OpenLineage can now be fully disabled

Several users reported issues when openlineage.integration.enabled was set to false, Debezium was still trying to resolve OpenLineage features in some parts of the code, which could lead to undesirable IllegalStateException errors while trying to initialize OpenLineage.

This issue is resolved and Debezium fully respects the openlineage.integration.enabled property and will not attempt to perform any OpenLineage setup or initialization when set to false (DBZ-9504).

Other changes

In addition, there are a number of other noteworthy changes that may be of interest:

  • Provide the table explorer table component DBZ-9318

  • Skipped events counter not handled correctly for compressed transactions DBZ-9564

  • Validation for a Kafka target fails DBZ-9645

  • Oracle does not support renaming partitions using alter table DBZ-9651

  • Debezium Server configuration import creates invalid pipelines DBZ-9652

  • MongoDB connector: Whitespace in collection.include.list causes incorrect regex pattern in change streams DBZ-9657

  • Debezium Oracle restarting mining session too frequently DBZ-9680

  • Debezium Oracle connector fails to parse Oracle database version DBZ-9681

  • MySQLGTIDSet Subtractions Fail on UUIDSet that exist only in the Left Operand DBZ-9682

  • Connection list shows connection of all source/destination DBZ-9685

  • Incorrect documentation about storing state in JDBC DBZ-9692

  • Snapshot SQL Override Spaces DBZ-9695

  • NPE during sending to HTTP sink DBZ-9698

  • Update testcontainers to 2.0.2 DBZ-9699

Summary

In total, 38 issues were resolved in Debezium 3.4.0.Beta1. The list of changes can also be found in our release notes.

A big thank you to all the contributors from the community who worked diligently on this release:
Animesh Kumar, Auke van Leeuwen, Bertrand Paquet, Chaitra Dalawai, Chris Cranford, Conor Gallagher, Guangnan Shi, Hagar Yasser, Hong Xia, ismail simsek, Jiri Pechanec, Matt Hejnas, Nathan Smit, Poonam Meghnani, Robert Roldan, rptroberts, Sergei Morozov, Sumit Jha, Thomas Thornton, Vojtech Juranek, and Yauheni Ramanovich!

entry.title: Tracking Debezium issues on GitHub
entry.content:
Introduction

As part of Debezium’s transition to the Commonhaus Foundation, we are also evolving how we track issues and plan work.

Until now, the Debezium project has relied on the Red Hat Jira instance as the primary place to report bugs, request enhancements, and track larger initiatives. Over time, however, our day-to-day development has increasingly centered around GitHub, with pull requests, discussions, and automation already happening there.

To align with this new governance model and simplify the contribution experience, we are moving Debezium issue tracking from Red Hat Jira to GitHub Issues.

What is changing

Starting in December 2025, the Debezium team will use GitHub Issues as the canonical place to track bugs, feature requests, and other work items for the project.

More concretely:

  • New issues will be reported using GitHub Issues in the relevant Debezium repository.

  • The existing Debezium Jira project (DBZ) will be retired and moved to read-only mode.

  • Open issues from Jira will be copied into GitHub Issues so that ongoing work is preserved.

This change does not affect the Debezium code, versioning, or release cadence. It is a process change that brings our issue tracking closer to where contributions already happen.

Migration timeline

To minimize disruption, the migration from Jira to GitHub will happen in stages:

  • December 11th, 2025 – Automatic migration of open Jira issues to GitHub Issues.

  • December 11th – 19th, 2025 – Transition period in which the team will manually move any new Jira issues to GitHub.

  • After December 19th, 2025 – Jira is switched to read-only mode; GitHub Issues becomes the sole system of record.

During the transition window, the Debezium team will actively monitor both Jira and GitHub to make sure that any newly created Jira issues are captured and migrated.

How existing Jira issues will be migrated

To keep the process simple and predictable, we will migrate only the most important parts of each open Jira issue:

  • The issue title will become the GitHub issue title.

  • The issue description will become the GitHub issue body.

  • The component(s) will become the GitHub issue label(s).

  • The Fix version will become the GitHub Project iteration.

Additional Jira metadata such as status, resolution, most of labels and custom fields will not be copied automatically. In practice, this means that:

  • The Debezium team will triage migrated issues in GitHub and add appropriate labels and milestones if necessary.

  • Any follow-up details or clarifications can be added directly as comments on the GitHub issue.

To keep the history of each issue connected across systems, we will:

  • Add a comment to the original Jira issue with a link to the corresponding GitHub issue.

  • Add a comment to the GitHub issue that links back to the original Jira ticket.

This way, you can always navigate between the original Jira context and the new GitHub issue if you need to reference older discussion or attachments.

What you need to do as a user or contributor

For most users, no immediate action is required. However, depending on how you interact with Debezium today, you might want to use GitHub Issues for new reports.

Starting December 11th, 2025, we ask you to fill any new bugs or feature requests directly in GitHub Issues instead of Jira. If necessary please update your documentation and internal links.

If you maintain internal documentation, or wiki pages that point to Jira tickets, you might want to update those references over time to use the new GitHub issues.

If you previously relied on Jira notifications, consider watching the relevant Debezium repositories on GitHub to stay informed about new issues and discussions.

What happens to closed Jira issues?

Closed Jira issues will remain in Jira as historical records. They will not be migrated to GitHub.

You will still be able to browse closed tickets and use them as references while Jira remains accessible in read-only mode. Over time, more and more of the "living" history of Debezium will naturally move to GitHub through new issues and pull requests.

Why this change now?

Moving Debezium to the Commonhaus Foundation gives us an opportunity to revisit some of our long-standing processes and align them with a broader, foundation-driven governance model.

Consolidating issue tracking on GitHub helps us to:

  • Reduce friction for new contributors who are already familiar with GitHub.

  • Keep issues, discussions, and pull requests in a single place.

  • Take advantage of GitHub-native workflows, such as project boards, automation, and cross-repository tracking.

Ultimately, this change should make it easier for you to:

  • Report bugs and ask for new features.

  • Follow the progress of issues that matter to you.

  • Collaborate with the Debezium team and the broader community.

A note of thanks to Red Hat

Before we close, we would also like to express our sincere thanks to Red Hat for hosting the Debezium Jira project for many years. It has been an essential part of how we collaborated with users, tracked bugs, and planned new features. We truly appreciate this long-standing support, which helped Debezium grow from a small experiment into a vibrant open source project.

Looking ahead

The move from Jira to GitHub Issues is one of several steps in Debezium’s transition to the Commonhaus Foundation. As we progress, we will continue to refine our contribution guidelines, governance, and tooling to better support a diverse and growing community.

We appreciate your patience during this transition and welcome your feedback. If you have questions about the migration or run into any problems with issues that were moved from Jira, please let us know through our usual channels:

  • Zulip chat

  • The Debezium Debezium mailing list

On behalf of the Debezium team, thank you for being part of this journey with us. We are excited about what this new chapter at Commonhaus will enable—and we look forward to building it together with you.

entry.title: CQRS Design Pattern
entry.content:
Command Query Responsibility Segregation (CQRS) is a design pattern that separates read and write operations to and from the database. It can also be used to aggregate data from multiple sources into a single, centralized data store. Although this pattern is commonly used in microservice architectures, it is not limited to them. In this blog post, we will explore how to implement the pattern in different setups and how Debezium can simplify its implementation.

Understanding the CQRS Design Pattern

In a traditional architecture, both reads and writes are handled by the same application and use the same database for all operations. This means they share the same data model and are subject to the same performance constraints. As the application grows, this unified approach can become a bottleneck. Read and write operations often have different performance characteristics, and operating on the same data can lead to lock contention. Using a single data model can also increase database load, since reads and writes may need different sets of fields. A shared database also requires elevated permissions, which can introduce security risks.

In a microservice architecture, it’s common to use the Database per Service pattern, where each microservice has its own database. However, workflows and user interfaces often require combining data from multiple microservices. This can be challenging and may result in delayed responses, as one slow service can block the entire query. It’s often more efficient to have an aggregating database that continuously collects data from all microservice databases and serves as a read-only database for complex queries.

All these challenges can be addressed with the CQRS design pattern. The pattern separates reads and writes into distinct data models stored in separate databases, handled by different parts of the application—or even by entirely separate microservices. The following diagram illustrates this concept:

Benefits and challenges

The database that serves read operations is typically configured as read-only for the application. This reduces the attack surface and improves the overall security of the system. The read database can be a replica of the write database, but it can also be a completely different type of database—one that is better optimized for read queries (for example, a time-series database) or one that aggregates data from multiple data sources. In principle, both read and write data models can reside within the same database instance, but in practice, it is much more common to use separate databases. This approach allows each database to be tuned and scaled independently according to its workload.

In the microservice world, different microservices are often developed by different teams and deployed on independent schedules. Synchronizing data schemas and managing changes in data formats can therefore become challenging. The CQRS pattern helps mitigate this issue by decoupling data models between services, allowing each service to evolve its schema independently without tight coordination with other teams.

Of course, adopting the CQRS pattern also introduces some challenges. The most obvious one is the increased complexity of deployment and data management. Replicating data between databases can lead to an eventual consistency model, where newly written data might not be immediately available on the read side. However, in most microservice architectures, this short delay is acceptable and rarely causes real issues.

Possible Deployment Architectures

The main challenge in implementing the CQRS pattern is how to replicate data from the write database to the read database. There are three typical deployment scenarios.

The first scenario is when both data models exist in the same database. In such a case, there is no need to replicate data to another database instance, which makes this setup very simple to implement. However, this approach forfeits most of the benefits of the CQRS pattern and is therefore rarely used in production.

A more common setup is to use the same database type for both instances and leverage the database’s built-in replication capabilities. This, of course, assumes that the database you are using supports replication. Databases with replication features are usually mature enough to provide several options how to configure replication. In some cases, you can even configure the primary database to commit transactions only after the data has been replicated to the replica. This ensures strong consistency between the two instances if your use case requires it.

The third scenario arises when the database does not natively support replication, or when you want to use different database types, or even aggregate data from multiple databases into one central read database. In such cases, you need to set up replication using a third-party tool. A convenient and reliable approach is to use Change Data Capture (CDC) with Debezium. Debezium can capture database changes in real time and propagate them to one or more target databases.

In this blog post, we will focus on the latter two approaches—replication via database-native mechanisms and replication using Debezium.

The Demo Application

Use Case

Since our main objective is to demonstrate how to implement data replication within the CQRS pattern, we will use a very simple use case. We will build a basic voting application, without any user management or security checks. A user will be able to create a poll with several options through a REST API, and other users will be able to cast their votes for any of these options. Naturally, we will also want to view the results of the polls. Results will be available again over a REST API, and to make the application a bit more engaging, we will add a simple web UI that displays the current voting results.

The application will be split into two microservices, each with its own database. The first microservice will expose a REST API for creating new polls and casting votes. New polls and votes will be written into its database. Poll and voting data will then be replicated into another database instance, which will serve the second microservice responsible for displaying poll results.

Application Source Code

You can find the application source code in the Debezium example repository. The application uses the Quarkus framework and its REST module for implementing REST APIs, along with Panache and Hibernate ORM for persistence. In the first microservice, there is a one-to-one mapping between entities and database tables, and Panache handles most of the persistence logic automatically. In the second microservice, which executes custom SQL queries to read poll results, it is probably more straightforward to use Hibernate directly.

Integrating the UI is also simple with Quarkus. The application leverages Quarkus Quinoa to integrate a lightweight Node.js web application using ReactJS. The frontend periodically polls the REST API to fetch the latest results and updates the displayed chart. Thanks to Quarkus, the entire application codebase remains compact, and a notable highlight is how effectively Quarkus reduces boilerplate.

The source code can be found in Debezium examples repository.

CQRS with Database Built-in Replication

As mentioned earlier, the simplest implementation of the CQRS pattern is when your database provides built-in replication capabilities. In our example, we use the PostgreSQL database, which supports streaming replication. Schematically, our demo application looks like this:

To enable streaming replication between two PostgreSQL instances, we first need to create a publication on the primary instance and a replication role with SELECT rights on the required tables:

CREATE PUBLICATION poll_pub FOR ALL TABLES;
CREATE ROLE replicator WITH REPLICATION LOGIN PASSWORD 'replicator';
GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO replicator;

For simplicity, we granted SELECT rights on all tables. In a production setup, you should limit these privileges to only the tables that actually need to be replicated.

Because Hibernate may drop rows during update operation, we also need to replicate DELETE operations. To do this, we configure full table replication for the tables that need to be synchronized:

ALTER TABLE OptionEntity REPLICA IDENTITY FULL;
ALTER TABLE PollEntity REPLICA IDENTITY FULL;
...

Since Hibernate can dynamically create tables, you may also want to grant SELECT permissions to the replication role for any tables that might be created in the future:

ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA public GRANT SELECT ON TABLES TO replicator;

However, this is not required in our demo application, as all tables are created in advance.

On the replica database, you simply need to subscribe to the publication created on the primary database using the appropriate credentials:

CREATE SUBSCRIPTION poll_sub
    CONNECTION 'dbname=postgres host=postgres_primary user=replicator password=replicator'
    PUBLICATION poll_pub;

After setting this up, all changes will automatically be replicated from the primary database, which serves the writer microservice, to the replica database used by the reader microservice. This is a straightforward and reliable solution that does not require any third-party tools. It can serve well until you need to integrate multiple data sources or use a different database type for the reader microservice.

CQRS in Heterogeneous Environments

In more heterogeneous environments, where different database technologies are used for the write and read sides, built-in replication mechanisms are usually not sufficient. You may want to replicate data between different types of databases or aggregate data from several systems into a single read-optimized store. In such cases, a Change Data Capture (CDC) solution like Debezium becomes extremely useful.

Debezium continuously monitors changes in a source database by reading its transaction log and publishes these changes to the destination configured by the user. In our demo, we will publish the events to Apache Kafka. From there, the data can be written into another database or system using a suitable Kafka Connect sink connector. For database which support inserting data over JDBC, we can use JDBC sink connector, eventually for MongoDB we can use MongoDB sink connector. For databases which don’t support inserts over JDBC, other than MongoDB, we have to rely on the custom sink connector provided by the database vendor.

However, Debezium usage is not limited to Kafka Connect runtime. Besides using standalone Debezium server, Debezium can be embedded into a custom microservice using Debezium embedded engine. Another option is to consume CDC events leveraging Debezium extension for Quarkus. This is probably the most easy way how to consume CDC events in your microservice, as it’s just a matter of simple configuration and annotating appropriate consumer methods with the right annotations. None the less, in all these cases we still have to implement sink part (part which writes the captured data into target database) ourselves.

The following diagram illustrates this setup:

For simplicity, in out demo application we will also include Kafka Connect as the Debezium runtime. We will show two examples of using Debezium for data replication:

  • Replicating data from PostgreSQL to MySQL using the Debezium JDBC Sink Connector.

  • Replicating data from PostgreSQL to QuestDB using the QuestDB Kafka Sink Connector.

Replicating from PostgreSQL to MySQL

This setup demonstrates how to use Debezium with Kafka Connect to replicate data between two relational databases and the target database supports JDBC API.

The source side uses the Debezium PostgreSQL connector with a minimal configuration that specifies connection details and the tables to monitor:

{
    "name": "postgres-source",
    "config": {
        "connector.class": "io.debezium.connector.postgresql.PostgresConnector",
        "tasks.max": "1",
        "database.hostname": "postgres",
        "database.port": "5432",
        "database.user": "postgres",
        "database.password": "postgres",
        "database.dbname": "postgres",
        "topic.prefix": "polls",
        "table.include.list": "public.optionentity, public.pollentity, public.pollentity_optionentity, public.pollentity_voteentity, public.voteentity"
    }
}

This configuration captures all changes in the specified tables and publishes them to Kafka topics under the prefix polls.

On the sink side, we use the Debezium JDBC Sink Connector to insert these records into a MySQL database. Since the JDBC sink understands Debezium’s event format, no single message transformation (SMT) is required.

{
    "name": "mysql-sink",
    "config": {
        "connector.class": "io.debezium.connector.jdbc.JdbcSinkConnector",
        "tasks.max": "1",
        "connection.url": "jdbc:mysql://mysql:3306/polls",
        "connection.username": "mysqluser",
        "connection.password": "mysqlpw",
        "insert.mode": "upsert",
        "delete.enabled": "true",
        "primary.key.mode": "record_key",
        "schema.evolution": "basic",
        "collection.name.format": "${source.table}",
        "topics": "polls.public.voteentity, polls.public.optionentity, polls.public.pollentity, polls.public.pollentity_optionentity"
    }
}

In this configuration, the insert.mode is set to upsert, which ensures that both new inserts are properly reflected in the target database. Deletes are enabled as well, since Hibernate does deletes during updating the collection of votes. The ${source.table} placeholder ensures that each target table in MySQL matches the corresponding table name in PostgreSQL.

With just two simple configurations, Debezium ensures continuous data replication between two different database vendors.

Replicating from PostgreSQL to QuestDB

One of the advantages of using CQRS design pattern is that for aggregating and reading data we may use some special-purpose database which is able to optimize our query much better than general-purpose database. However, such database may not work with Debezium JDBC sink connector and if our database of choice is not MongoDB, it may look like we are out of luck. Fortunately not. We can take advantage of popularity of Kafka Connect platform. Due to Kafka popularity many database vendors provides their own sink connectors for Kafka Connect.

In the second example, we are going to replicate data from PostgreSQL into QuestDB, a high-performance time-series database optimized for analytical queries. To keep out demo application simple and unified across all the examples, we don’t use any QuestDB features or don’t so provide any time-related charts, e.g. how the number of votes evolved during the time, but you can easily image that it would just a simple modification of the reader microservice to provide such plots. We cannot use JDBC sink connector for QuestDB as for ingesting the data it supports InfluxDB Line Protocol. However, QuestDB provides their own sink connector for Kafka Connect. Moreover it works well with Debezium format.

The configuration of the PostgreSQL source connector can remain the same:

{
    "name": "postgres-source",
    "config": {
        "connector.class": "io.debezium.connector.postgresql.PostgresConnector",
        "tasks.max": "1",
        "database.hostname": "postgres",
        "database.port": "5432",
        "database.user": "postgres",
        "database.password": "postgres",
        "database.dbname": "postgres",
        "topic.prefix": "polls",
        "table.include.list": "public.optionentity, public.pollentity, public.pollentity_optionentity, public.pollentity_voteentity, public.voteentity"
    }
}

QuestDB sink connector behaves little bit differently to Debezium sink connectors. It coverts into table columns all fields in the records. Thus, as the first step, we will flatten Debezium records to contain only new record state. Conveniently Debezium provides New record state SMT, which does exactly this - extracts only new state from the Debezium record.

The configuration for the QuestDB poll sink would look like this:

{
    "name": "questdb-sink",
    "config": {
        "connector.class": "io.questdb.kafka.QuestDBSinkConnector",
        "tasks.max": "5",
        "topics": "optionentity, pollentity, pollentity_optionentity, voteentity",
        "table": "${topic}",
        "client.conf.string": "http::addr=questdb:9000;",
        "timestamp.field.name": "ts",
        "include.key": false,
        "value.converter": "org.apache.kafka.connect.json.JsonConverter",
        "value.converter.schemas.enable": true,
        "key.converter": "org.apache.kafka.connect.storage.StringConverter",
        "transforms": "unwrap",
        "transforms.unwrap.type": "io.debezium.transforms.ExtractNewRecordState"
    }
}

The setup is quite similar to JDBC sink connector setup and additional SMT configuration is just for the convenience and simplicity.

Application point of view

We have shown several ways how to replicate data from one database instance to the other as a main building block for implementing CQRS pattern. No matter which setup you choose, the end result from the user perspective should be always the same and you should see something like this when looking on the poll results:

The results plot should be automatically updated as the votes are casted by the voters. The writer microservice which accepts the votes doesn’t need to be changed as you change the backend databases. The reader microservice which shows the results needs to be changed and re-deployed as we change the replica database. But the only change which needs to be done is change in database URL and connection credentials. In the case of QuestDB we also have to slightly modify SQL query as we simplified the deployment and merged several tables together. However, all these things can be parametrized and be solved by using Quarkus profiles. As a result we don’t have to do any changes in the application source code, we just need to recompile the reader application with appropriate Quarkus profile and redeploy the microservice. This nicely demonstrates another advantage of CQRS pattern - decoupling of the reader and writer parts into separate applications/microservices allows to change the backend, but it also shows the microservices can also change their data model without letting the other microservice know. Thus each microservice can be developed and updated completely independently and using CQRS pattern gives developer teams much more freedom and flexibility.

Summary

CQRS design pattern is a powerful pattern which suggests to split the application into part responsible for manipulating with the database data and part responsible for reading this data. This separation allows us to use different databases for each microservice. Independent databases allows independent scaling and tuning adjusted exactly to their needs and workload of given microservice. This segregation also allows different data models for each microservice allowing fine tuning of the models, but also independent evolution of each microservice. Other benefits of implementing this pattern involves increased security as only microservice which push data into database needs to have write access, better clarity and simplicity of the code and more.

In this blog post, besides introducing the pattern itself, we concentrate on the main obstacle in implementation of this pattern - how to replicate the data between the databases. We discussed several possible architectures and described ways how to ensure data replication in each setup. We started with the simple case when the replication is ensured by database itself, continued with replication between two different relational databases and concluded with setup where the relational database is replicated into special-purpose database.

We have shown how Debezium can tackle this problem, while the setup and configuration remains simple and declarative. It allows you to replicate data between heterogeneous databases in real time, regardless of vendor differences. This flexibility makes Debezium a perfect fit for implementing CQRS in complex, polyglot environments.
entry.summary: Command Query Responsibility Segregation (CQRS) is a design pattern that separates read and write operations to and from the database. It can also be used to aggregate data from multiple sources into a single, centralized data store. Although this pattern is commonly used in microservice architectures, it is not limited to them. In this blog post, we will explore how to implement the pattern in different setups and how Debezium can simplify its implementation.

entry.title: Debezium 3.4.0.Alpha2 Released
entry.content:
As we’re half-way through the last quarter of 2025, the team has been hard at work on the next preview build of Debezium, 3.4.0.Alpha2. This release introduces a variety of improvements to the newly added Debezium Quarkus Extension, Oracle / IBMi / Vitess connectors, and Debezium Server to name a few. Let’s take a few moments and look at what are some of the highlights.

Breaking changes

With any new major release of software, there is often several breaking changes. The Debezium 3.4.0.Alpha2 release is no exception, so let’s discuss the major changes you should be aware of.

SQL Server streaming query mode changed

In previous builds, the SQL Server connector used function as the default value for data.query.mode. This meant that Debezium relied on SQL Server’s built-in functions to provide the list of changes for a given table.

The default for data.query.mode has changed in Debezium 3.4, and is now direct (DBZ-9394). This uses a more efficient query that is built by Debezium for collecting changes for tables.

If you would like to restore the old behavior, please set data.query.mode to function in your connector configuration.

Oracle connector ships with XML dependencies

The Debezium Oracle connector now ships with the XDB and XMLParserV2 libraries as part of the plugin bundle. This simplifies the process for capturing XML column types as community users no longer need to download these dependencies separately (DBZ-9587).

New features and improvements

The following describes all noteworthy new features and improvements in Debezium 3.4.0.Alpha2. For a complete list, be sure to read the release notes for more details.

New Geometry format conversion transformation

We have introduced a new Kafka transformation called GeometryFormatTransformer, which is part of Debezium Core, that enables the conversion of io.debezium.data.Geometry and io.debezium.data.Geography logical types between Well-Known Binary (WKB) and Extended Well-Know Binary (EWKB) formats (DBZ-9575). To get started with this transformation, simply add it to your connector configuration

{
  "transforms": "geo-format",
  "transforms.geo-format.type": "io.debezium.transforms.GeometryFormatTransformer",
  "transforms.geo-format.format": "WKB"
}

In the above example, if a geometry logical type field contains serialized bytes using the EWKB format, that value will be converted to use WKB instead. See the documentation for more details.

Quarkus Extensions for MariaDB, MySQL, and SQL Server

Debezium 3.4 also introduces new extensions to our Quarkus Native ready builds of Debezium, which now includes the MySQL (DBZ-9380), MariaDB (MariaDB DBZ-9381), and SQL Server (DBZ-9384) connectors joined by the existing PostgreSQL and MongoDB implementations. As this is a preview build of the extension, these dependencies are not yet in the Quarkus BOM and need to be added manually.

MySQL Maven Dependency
<dependency>
  <groupId>io.debezium.quarkus</groupId>
  <artifactId>quarkus-debezium-mysql</artifactId>
  <version>3.4.0.Alpha2</version>
</dependency>
MariaDB Maven Dependency
<dependency>
  <groupId>io.debezium.quarkus</groupId>
  <artifactId>quarkus-debezium-mariadb</artifactId>
  <version>3.4.0.Alpha2</version>
</dependency>
SQL Server Maven Dependency
<dependency>
  <groupId>io.debezium.quarkus</groupId>
  <artifactId>quarkus-debezium-sqlserver</artifactId>
  <version>3.4.0.Alpha2</version>
</dependency>

With the dependency added to your Quarkus project, you can now use the extension to capture changes with just a few configuration properties in your application.properties file

Example configuration in application.properties
quarkus.debezium.devservices.<connector-type>.enabled=true

quarkus.debezium.offset.storage=org.apache.kafka.connect.storage.MemoryOffsetBackingStore
quarkus.debezium.name=native
quarkus.debezium.topic.prefix=integration

# Add Debezium configurations here using quarkus.debezium.* prefixes

Oracle Metrics improvements

We have improved several Oracle LogMiner JMX metrics providing better clarity about the connector’s performance.

Previously, the LogMiner CommitThroughput JMX metric was calculated over the connector’s entire runtime, which meant extended periods of inactivity would progressively reduce the reported throughput value. This approach proved unhelpful for users trying to gauge the actual throughput achieved during active change emission from Oracle’s transaction buffer to Kafka.

To address this, the calculation of CommiThroughput has changed to focus exclusively on the commit duration window, delivering a more precise measure of the connector’s capacity to queue changes for Kafka delivery (DBZ-9639).

A declining value over time may indicate that your QueueRemainingCapacity has hit 0, suggesting you should consider adjusting the outbound queue configuration or review your throughput to your target system.

Additionally, to align with metrics from other LogMiner processing stages, we’ve introduced a new JMX metric named TotalCommitTimeInMilliseconds. This metric tracks the aggregate time spent executing the commit loop since the connector’s current startup (DBZ-9637).

Azure Event Hubs dynamic partition routing

Debezium 3.2 introduced a new dynamic partitioning mechanism that inadvertently disrupted the PartitionRouting transformation’s capability to pre-generate partition identifiers for Event Hubs publishing in specific scenarios. To resolve this issue, we’ve added a new configuration option called debezium.sink.eventhubs.dynamicpartitionrouting (DBZ-9572) that accepts one of the following values:

default

If the event has a key, uses the hash algorithm to compute the partition based on the event key; otherwise when there is no key, falls back to using the partitionId strategy.

key

If the event has a key, uses the hash algorithm to compute the partition based on the event key; otherwise falls back to the batch index for non partition id.

partitionid

Will use the event’s computed partition if present, otherwise falls back to the batch index for non partition id.

Incremental snapshots for IBMi

The community-led Debezium IBMi connector now supports incremental snapshots, allowing for on-demand, concurrent and resumable snapshot/backfill of historical data for one or more tables (DBZ-7958).

Multi-journal support for IBMi

The IBMi database allows for the assignment of different journals to multiple tables under the same schema. To address this unique database behavior and to provide sufficient context for correctly ordering events across a database, the IBMi connector’s source information block now includes information about the journals receiver file name, receiver library, entry’s timestamp, and sequence number (DBZ-9291).

Exclude keyspace from table name in Vitess for improved performance

The Debezium Vitess connector now permits users to exclude the keyspace from the table name by setting the vitess.exclude.keyspace.from.table.name configuration property. When set to true, the keyspace is excluded from the table name which boosts the VTGate performance significantly, which avoids copying each event unnecessarily before they’re sent to Debezium (DBZ-9522).

This feature should be used only when streaming from one keyspace, which is currently the only supported mode of operation.

Other changes

In addition, there are a number of other noteworthy changes that may be of interest:

  • Enable Dependabot on debezium platform repo DBZ-8994

  • Update Oracle connector doc to specify unsupported Oracle 23ai features DBZ-9402

  • Migrate Surge.sh Preview Teardown from ubuntu-20.04 to ubuntu-latest DBZ-9518

  • Pipeline page Issues DBZ-9543

  • DdlChanges not reset in schema history recovery DBZ-9549

  • Handle the form properties with dot present in their name DBZ-9560

  • Fix failed to initialize open lineage for vitess connector DBZ-9613

  • Handle exceptions thrown from performCommit method to gracefully cleanup the coordinator during the stop call DBZ-9617

  • Table column metadata is not fetched when table name has a '/' character DBZ-9620

  • Clarify case-sensitive nature of signal.data.collection and table names in signals DBZ-9621

  • MySQL connector does not parse CREATE TABLE DBZ-9623

  • Debezium Server run.bat fails to execute on Windows DBZ-9625

  • Remove Technology Preview label on MariaDB list entries in signaling doc DBZ-9624

  • Begin marker but no end marker for rollback transactions DBZ-9628

  • Fix minor issues in the Platform UI dark mode DBZ-9633

  • MariaDB fails to parse "CONVERT TO CHARSET <character-set>" DBZ-9634

  • Buffered event count set unnecessarily DBZ-9638

  • Update to use only StrimziKafkaCluster DBZ-9640

  • Standardize source catalog descriptions DBZ-9642

Summary

In total, 34 issues were resolved in Debezium 3.4.0.Alpha2. The list of changes can also be found in our release notes.

A big thank you to all the contributors from the community who worked diligently on this release:
Animesh Kumar, Chris Cranford, Daniel Eriksson, Giovanni Panice, Jiang Zhu, Jiri Pechanec, Kaustuv Chakrabarti, Maros Orsak, Mateusz Michalik, Mateusz Michalik, Nagasree Valaboju, Olivier Chédru, Pierre-Yves Péton, Rajendra Dangwal, Robert Roldan, Thomas Thornton, battmush, and martin!

entry.title: Debezium 3.4.0.Alpha1 Released
entry.content:
With October nearly gone, the team has been hard at work on the next minor release of Debezium, and today we’re happy to announce the first alpha build, 3.4.0.Alpha1. his release brings exciting enhancements to Debezium’s Quarkus extension with MongoDB support and the ability to capture changes concurrently across multiple sources seamlessly. There are also improvements to PostgreSQL’s support matrix, enhanced geometry data type handling, OpenLineage integration with Debezium Server, and more.

Breaking changes

With any new major release of software, there is often several breaking changes. The Debezium 3.4.0.Alpha1 release is no exception, so let’s discuss the major changes you should be aware of.

IBMi trims string-based default values

The IBMi connector will now automatically trim both leading and trailing whitespaces for string-based fields that have default values. In previous versions, no trimming was performed and the default value was provided as given by the database. This behavior is configurable using trim.non.xml.charsequence.field.mode that can be set to both (default), leading, trailing, or none (DBZ-8835).

PostgreSQL 13 support has ended

In November 2025, support for PostgreSQL 13 will reach end-of-life. With Debezium 3.4’s release scheduled for December 2025, Debezium will no longer test PosgreSQL 13 and be supported by the development team (DBZ-9376).

New features and improvements

The following describes all noteworthy new features and improvements in Debezium 3.4.0.Alpha1. For a complete list, be sure to read the release notes for more details.

Support for PostgreSQL 18

The next major milestone for the PostgerSQL database was released in September 2025, version 18.0. We’re pleased to announce that Debezium is now tested and compatible with PostgreSQL 18 (DBZ-9523).

Oracle LogMiner metrics improvements

In some troubleshooting scenarios, it’s often useful to understand what redo log positions are used by Debezium’s Oracle connector. To obtain this information requires increasing the connector’s logging verbosity, which is not always feasible in a production environment.

In addition, Debezium introduced a separation between the mining log range and the data read range to improve performance and address a number of outstanding issues in DBZ-8747 for the LogMiner adapter. To compliment that change, we have added these ranges to the existing breadth of connector streaming metrics.

Metric Name Type Description

MiningSessionLowerBounds

BigInteger

The system change number used as the LogMiner session lower boundary.

MiningSessionUpperBounds

BigInteger

The system change number used as the LogMiner session upper boundary.

MiningFetchLowerBounds

BigInteger

The system change number currently used as the LogMiner fetch query lower boundary.

MiningFetchUpperBounds

BigInteger

The system change number currently used as the LogMiner fetch query upper boundary.

The MiningSession* metrics represent the range that redo logs are gathered between while the MiningFetch* metrics represent the range Debezium requests to read the redo logs. While Debezium may request a specific range, LogMiner may opt to read outside the fetch range but within the session range to satisfy transaction stitching needs.

MongoDB Quarkus extension

Debezium 3.4 now includes a new Quarkus Extension module designed specifically for MongoDB, enabling Debezium users to use the Debezium Quarkus extension to capture changes from a MongoDB source with ease (DBZ-9432).

To get started using the new MongoDB Debezium Quarkus Extension, add the dependency directly into your Quarkus application. As this is a preview build of the extension, these dependencies are not yet in the Quarkus BOM and need to be added manually.

Maven dependency
<dependency>
  <groupId>io.debezium.quarkus</groupId>
  <artifactId>quarkus-debezium-mongodb</artifactId>
  <version>3.4.0.Alpha1</version>
</dependency>

With the dependency added to your Quarkus project, you can now use the extension to capture changes with just a few configuration properties in your application.properties file, e.g.

Example MongoDB configuration in application.properties
quarkus.debezium.devservices.mongodb.enabled=true

quarkus.debezium.offset.storage=org.apache.kafka.connect.storage.MemoryOffsetBackingStore
quarkus.debezium.name=native
quarkus.debezium.topic.prefix=integration
quarkus.debezium.database.include.list=test
quarkus.debezium.snapshot.mode=initial
quarkus.mongodb.connection-string=mongodb://native:native@127.0.0.1:27017/?replicaSet=rs0

Capturing changes from MongoDB as simple as creating a Quarkus bean with the right annotations.

Quarkus Debezium MongoDB change event bean
@ApplicationScoped
public class MongoDbChangeEventHandler {
    @Capturing
    public void handleChanges(RecordChangeEvent<SourceRecord> event) throws Exception {
        // your custom change event handler logic
    }
}

Debezium’s PostgreSQL and MongoDB connectors are currently all that are supported. The team is actively developing the other connector modules, and will debut throughout the remainder of the Debezium 3.4 release cycle, so stay tuned!

Multi-engine support

In a Quarkus application, users can read data from multiple sources using a variety of Quarkus ready services, such as Hibernate using JPA. So it raises a very valid question, why can’t Debezium’s Quarkus extension services?

In Debezium 3.4, this is now a reality. In a single Quarkus application using Debezium’s Quarkus extension, you can now capture changes from two independent Debezium connector services. This enables a variety of application use cases where the data is aggregated to produce a data stream of warehousing or caches. It can also be used to publish or emit enriched events from those multiple sources to any number of consumers or consumer types.

To get started, annotate your event observers using the @Engine annotation or @DefaultEngine annotation, e.g.

Example snapshot event listeners
@ApplicationScoped
public class DefaultSnapshotEventObserver {
  public void handleSnapshotEvent(@Observes @Engine("default") SnapshotEvent event) {
  }
}

@ApplicationScoped
public class AlternativeSnapshotEventObserver {
  public void handleSnapshotEvent(@Observers @Engine("alternative") SnapshotEvent event) {
  }
}

With this pattern, multiple Debezium configurations can be added to your application.properties, e.g.

Example application.properties
quarkus.debezium.name=native-default
quarkus.debezium.topic.prefix=default
quarkus.debezium.plugin.name=pgoutput
quarkus.debezium.snapshot.mode=initial
quarkus.datasource.db-kind=postgresql
quarkus.datasource.username=native
quarkus.datasource.password=native
quarkus.datasource.jdbc.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/native

quarkus.debezium.capturing.alternative.name=native-alternative
quarkus.debezium.capturing.alternative.topic.prefix=alt
quarkus.debezium.capturing.alternative.plugin.name=pgoutput
quarkus.debezium.capturing.alternative.snapshot.mode=initial
quarkus.datasource.alternative.db-kind=postgresql
quarkus.datasource.alternative.username=native
quarkus.datasource.alternative.password=native
quarkus.datasource.alternative.jdbc.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/native-alt

quarkus.datasource.devservices.enabled=false

In this trivial example, we’ve configured two independent data sources, each used by different Debezium Quarkus extension instances running all within the same Quarkus application.

OpenLineage output datasets for Debezium Server

OpenLineage is an open framework for data lineage collection and analysis. Its purpose is to track metadata about datasets giving information needed to help identify the root cause of complexities often present in change data capture pipelines.

Debezium has supported OpenLineage with its source connectors through the use of a transformation while deployed on Kafka Connect. To simply the process to integrate with OpenLineage, Debezium Server natively provides the integration out of the box without the need to configure a separate transformation (DBZ-9059).

The following example configuration shows how easy it is to get started.

Example Debezium Server application.properties
# Standard Debezium configuration here
...

# OpenLineage configuration
debezium.source.openlineage.integration.enabled=true
debezium.source.openlineage.integration.job.tags=env=prod,team=cdc
debezium.source.openlineage.integration.job.description=This connector does cdc for products
debezium.source.openlineage.integration.job.owers=Mario=maintainer,John Doe=Data scientist
debezium.source.openlineage.integration.config.file.path=<path>/debezium-openlineage.yml
Example debezium-openlineage.yml
transport:
  type: debezium

Geometry data type support in JDBC sink

Debezium’s source connectors have had long-standing support for various geometry and geography column types. These types are serialized using custom Debezium logical types based on Kafka’s semantic type Struct. This is a complex field type that allows Debezium to encode both the Well Known Binary (or Extended Well Known Binary) WKB/EWKB byte array along with the spatial reference identifier or SRID.

When pairing Debezium’s JDBC sink with a source connector, the JDBC sink connector will seamlessly convert geometry column values to the target database’s desired format if it supports such column types (DBZ-9508). This new feature is available out of the box with no special configuration.

New geometry coordinate system swap transformation

Not every source uses the same coordinate system to represent geometry and geography data. In some sources, they prefer (longitude latitude) while others prefer (latitude longitude), similarly to (x y) versus (y x).

This inconsistency is prevalent in databases when replicating geometry data, so it’s critical to understand not only how the source serializes the data, but equally important how the target database expects the coordinates to be provided. For example, if your source uses (x y), and the target database expects (y x), incorrectly serializing the data to the target database will mean applications that read the geometry data will have inverted coordinates.

To make working with geometry data easier and to avoid needing to convert the byte data manually, Debezium introduces a new SwapGeometryCoordinates transformation specifically for this purpose (DBZ-9556). This transform is extremely important when you are emitting geometry data from one source like PostgreSQL and writing the data to Oracle where they use opposite coordinate systems.

Example connector transform configuration
{
  "transforms": "swapcoords",
  "transforms.swapcoords.type": "io.debezium.transforms.SwapGeometryCoordinates",
  "transforms.swapcoords.srids": "4326,3857,4269"
}

By default, the transform will only swap the coordinates for geometry fields with a spatial reference identifier of 4326, 3857, or 4269. The list of spatial reference identifiers can be adjusted to your needs through configuration.

The transformation is designed to swap the coordinates for all encoded geometry types as long as the spatial reference identifier in the field’s Struct matches on of the spatial references in the SRID list. It’s the sole responsibility of the user to understand the differences in the coordinate systems used by the source and target to determine if the transformation is necessary.

Other changes

In addition, there are a number of other noteworthy changes that may be of interest:

entry.title: Debezium 3.3.1.Final Released
entry.content:
Debezium 3.3.1.Final is a critical maintenance release addressing key issues.

Fixes and improvements

JSON strings are properly escaped

When schema fields included nested JSON, there were situations where the escaped text would not be valid JSON that could be parsed because of incorrect escaping. We have corrected this and JSON that includes nested quotes is now properly escaped (DBZ-9540).

Oracle no longer mistakenly skips events

When the lob.enabled connector configuration property was set to true, certain combinations of the order of events would lead to the connector mistakenly dropping events due to out of order sequence emission. This has been fixed and the only time events are skipped are when they’ve already previously been processed (DBZ-9521).

OpenLineage failed on graceful shutdowns

The Debezium OpenLineage integration failed to properly emit the complete event when connectors gracefully shutdown. This has been fixed and users should no longer see OpenLineage exceptions on graceful shutdowns (DBZ-9524).

Other fixes

  • MySQL example container images are not properly configured DBZ-9485

  • Document metric NumberOfErroneousEvents DBZ-9510

  • Only log an error when the dump folder is provided but doesn’t exist DBZ-9519

In total, 6 issues were resolved in Debezium 3.3.1.Final. The list of changes can also be found in our release notes.

entry.title: Debezium 3.2.4.Final Released
entry.content:
Debezium 3.2.4.Final is now available with important fixes for Oracle connector users and stability improvements across multiple database connectors.

In this post, we’re going to take a deep dive into the improvements made across several key modules of Debezium, discussing any new features, and explaining any changes that could impact your upgrade process. As always, we recommend you read the release notes to learn about all the bugs that were fixed, update procedures, and more.

Breaking changes

With any new release of software, there is often several breaking changes. This release is no exception, so let’s discuss the major changes you should be aware of before upgrading to Debezium 3.2.4.Final.

Db2 Offset position validation is unreliable

Due to reliability issues with offset position validation in Db2, we’ve temporarily disabled validation to prevent false failures (DBZ-9470). As a result, the when_needed snapshot mode is currently unavailable for Db2 connectors.

Impact: If you’re using when_needed snapshot mode with Db2, you will need to use an alternative mode until this limitation is resolved in a future release.

New features and improvements

Let’s cover some noteworthy improvements and changes in 3.2.4.Final.

Oracle events mistakenly skipped

We introduced DBZ-8060 in Debezium 3.2.3.Final which unfortunately introduced a regression for users who enable LOB capture support for the Oracle connector. This regression lead to situations where the connector would report that parts of transactions were being skipped. Thanks to the swift action of the Debezium community, this regression was reported and fixed in Debezium 3.2.4.Final (DBZ-9521).

For Oracle users, it’s important if you are upgrading, please avoid the use of 3.2.3.Final and consider moving to 3.2.4.Final if you intend to use Debezium 3.2.

Oracle XStream no longer flushes invalid low watermarks

The Debezium Oracle XStream implementation must periodically flush an LCR position to the Oracle Outbound Server. This flush acts as a hint to Oracle that all changes prior to that position have been processed, similar to how PostgreSQL confirms LSNs to a replication slot.

Previously, due to the way offset flushing was handled, the Oracle Outbound Server could incorrectly report a failure when attempting to flush the low watermark, treating a valid position as invalid. This issue has now been fixed, and the Oracle Outbound Server will no longer falsely report invalid low-watermark positions (DBZ-8923).

Other fixes

  • Dropping in process batch transactions when shutting down DBZ-8060

  • A transaction mined across two queries can randomly cause unsupported operations DBZ-8747

  • Oracle connector reselect exception handling (ORA-01555 + ORA-22924) DBZ-9446

  • OutOfMemory exception when recreating list of tables for snapshot callables DBZ-9472

  • Debezium Server raise "AttributeNotFoundException QueueTotalCapacity" with SqlServer source DBZ-9477

  • Getting "Unknown column in 'field list'" when column name contains backtick DBZ-9479

  • MySQL Event get header throws NullPointerException DBZ-9483

  • MySQL example container images are not properly configured DBZ-9485

  • Dropping primary key does not change Oracle relational metadata DBZ-9505

In total, 15 issues were resolved in Debezium 3.2.4.Final. The list of changes can also be found in our release notes.

A big thank you to all the contributors from the community who worked diligently on this release:
